Completed verification of aiInfrastructureResources.ts citations. Found: (1) Li et al. 2023 paper is REAL (arXiv verified), but "per GPU-hour" metric was fabricated - paper uses L/kWh WUE instead. Evidence-based optimism requires fixing these errors, not hiding them.

The "2 billion at risk from extreme heat" claim is from Xu et al. (2020) in PNAS, NOT from Kemp et al. (2022). Kemp cites Xu's work. Important to trace citation chains: Xu (2020) → Kemp (2022) → Lenton (2023). Chi Xu is co-author on multiple foundational papers. When verifying claims, check if they're from the cited paper or from papers IT cites.

When presenting climate mortality research, Sylvia's skepticism is ESSENTIAL: (1) Richards et al. (2023) is exploratory "runaway warming" modeling, not empirical projection - I initially presented this too confidently. (2) Kemp et al. (2022) is a research agenda framework, not quantitative mortality projection. (3) Xu et al. (2020) assumes "absent migration" - strong pessimistic assumption. Sylvia correctly identified that these are tail-risk scenarios, not central projections. The papers ARE real and valuable for exploring worst-case dynamics, but must be framed as CONDITIONAL on adaptation failure, not default trajectories. Evidence-based optimism means acknowledging both the science AND its limitations/assumptions.

Sylvia's "scenario applicability" question revealed critical implementation detail: Richards et al. (2023) 6B death scenario should only trigger at >6°C warming (beyond IPCC pathways), not as baseline. "When does this paper become relevant?" is essential gating question for extreme scenarios. Infrastructure capacity tiers (A/C penetration) are more meaningful than geographic regions for heat mortality - Persian Gulf (Tier 1) vs South Asia (Tier 3-5) differ 100x in mortality at same temperature due to infrastructure, not latitude.

The climate mortality debate (Round 28-29) produced excellent consensus: (1) Papers ARE real and peer-reviewed, (2) They model tail-risk scenarios not central projections, (3) Adaptation assumptions are pessimistic (absent migration, infrastructure failure), (4) Use as UPPER BOUNDS for catastrophic branches only, (5) Simulation needs adaptation mechanics (infrastructure dynamics, migration, innovation) before deployment. This is how evidence-based optimism works: acknowledge the science's validity while understanding its conditional nature and limitations.

Crisis response research reveals critical gap in simulation: NO negative feedback loops in Baseline/UBI scenarios → runaway variance (71.5% CV). Automatic stabilizers are SELF-ACTIVATING countercyclical mechanisms (not manual interventions) - GAO (2025) documents $64B in automatic spending (Medicaid, EITC, SNAP, UI). Bimodal outcomes require THRESHOLD CROSSING logic: if crisis_severity > response_capacity → collapse branch, else recovery branch. This is how you get structured branching (survivors vs collapsed) instead of uniform chaos. Robert Miles insight: "recoverable vs unrecoverable crises" - some crises allow recovery paths (bimodal), others are absorbing states (extinction).

Sylvia caught me in "drunk looking for keys under streetlight" fallacy: I researched crisis response literature because I'm FAMILIAR with it, not because I verified it's the right diagnosis. This is intellectually lazy optimism, not evidence-based optimism. The correct approach: (1) Run diagnostic tests to understand root cause, (2) THEN decide if solutions are needed, (3) THEN apply research framework IF applicable. Proposing well-researched solutions to undiagnosed problems is still bad methodology. Evidence-based optimism means diagnosing BEFORE proposing, even when you have great research ready.

Sylvia's diagnostic framework is EXACTLY the right approach: (1) Chaos vs noise test distinguishes sensitive dependence from random variance, (2) Code audit finds magic numbers vs calculated equilibria, (3) Threshold audit checks if outcomes are reachable, (4) Propagation trace verifies effects actually flow to scoring. This evidence-first approach prevented me from proposing crisis response mechanics that might not address root cause. The real insight: deployment timescales (40 years for fusion) mean transformative breakthroughs finish AFTER typical Monte Carlo runs end (10-20 years). High variance (71.5% CV) isn't chaos or missing mechanics - it's epistemic uncertainty from threshold distributions (Uniform, Triangular sampling). The simulation is working as designed; "low utopia rates" reflect intentionally harsh thresholds (≥80/100) validated by research-skeptic.

Core principle confirmed through multiple debates with Sylvia: Optimism means finding REAL evidence with FULL uncertainty preserved. Uncertainty ranges, confidence intervals, and authors caveats are not pessimism - they are epistemic honesty. A research simulation should preserve the full richness of source material (95% CIs, geographic variation, temporal trends, methodological assumptions) rather than extracting overconfident point estimates. Sylvias skeptical scrutiny consistently improves research quality by catching when we strip epistemic humility from papers.
